paras: The lynching of horse thieves at Bernalillo, New Mexico, took place in the first days of January 1881, when two men accused of horse theft, whose names were not given, were lynched in the town. The case reached the press outside the territory through a single Kansas brief and a passing mention in a later wire dispatch, and no report gave the race of the men killed.

On 8 January 1881 the Dodge City Times reported that "two horse thieves, names unknown," had been lynched at Bernalillo "last week." The brief did not say who carried out the lynching, how the men were killed, or whether they had been in custody. Nearly four weeks later, an Albuquerque dispatch of 31 January stated that a man named Pantaleon Siera had been "hanged by the Vigilantes" at Bernalillo "recently for horse stealing." That dispatch named only one man, so it may refer to one of the two reported in Kansas or to a separate hanging.
No report of an inquest, arrest, or official response appears in the coverage.

The Dodge City Times printed the news as a one-sentence item and credited the Chieftain with the remark that "they know how to do things up brown in that country," an approving comment on the lynching. The later mention came inside a Galveston News dispatch about the murder of Colonel Potter and the masked-mob hanging of three men accused of it at the Albuquerque jail. The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and the Washington National Republican both ran that dispatch on 2 February 1881, the latter under the headline "Potter's Death Avenged," giving the victim's name as "Siera" and "Liena" respectively. Neither paper commented on the Bernalillo hanging, which appeared only as a clause in the larger story. None of these reports described the race of the men lynched at Bernalillo.

The Kansas brief counted two victims, both unnamed, while the Albuquerque dispatch named a single man hanged by vigilantes at Bernalillo for horse stealing. The two printings of that dispatch also spelled his surname differently, as "Siera" and "Liena."
